title: Turned away by a white arranger; learning to write arrangements
summary: A white arranging office changes its tone when it sees they are Black musicians, so Wooding begins writing whole arrangements himself.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, I'll tell you Chris, we went downtown one day and we was trying to get some arrangements, because at that time I was only making introductions and endings. But inside the strain I wasn't doing it, you see.

And you see, now, so we'd call up, I forget whose arranging office it was. A white arranger's office. And I said, 'We'd like to come down and see about getting some arrangements.' He said, 'Sure, we've got plenty of time.' But he didn't know at the time that we were black musicians. So, when we hit the door, his attitude altogether changed. He said, 'Oh, oh, what do you want?' 'Somebody told us to come down here and get some arrangements.' So he said, 'No, I don't see how nobody could say that, because we've got all the work we can do.' So, and the way he talked, I knew he wasn't telling the truth. So we said, 'Okay buddy, it's alright.' So we come out and went on uptown. And then, from then on, I started thinking in terms of the whole number. And I ended up making numbers like, 'Gee, But I'm Glad to Know It's the Old Gang of

Mine". I started making the "Covered Wagon". And such things like that. And I was doing a nice job, 'cause course, right away. I always believed in making an arrangement according to what the words of the song was, see?
